subsystems.name: Micro-agent body
subsystems.role: the individual particle — everything else is attached to it.
parts: polymer or silica bead, or folded DNA structure
asymmetric shape to break symmetry for propulsion
surface attachment points for payloads

subsystems.name: Propulsion and actuation
subsystems.role: makes a particle move when no propeller can be machined at this scale.
parts: magnetic layer steered by external field coils
catalytic surface (e.g. platinum) that decomposes a fuel into a jet
acoustic response to an ultrasound field
flexible flagella-like tail driven externally

subsystems.name: Payload and effector
subsystems.role: what the swarm actually does at the target.
parts: drug or enzyme cargo
receptor or antibody on the surface
mechanically active element such as a pH- or enzyme-triggered switch

subsystems.name: Local sensing and signalling
subsystems.role: lets agents react to their neighbours and surroundings without a central controller.
parts: chemical gradient sensors (receptors)
quorum-sensing-like threshold switches
release of signalling molecules as a trail

subsystems.name: Swarm control layer
subsystems.role: turns millions of dumb agents into one coherent action.
parts: stigmergy rules: agents modify the environment, and the modified environment steers later agents
ant-colony-optimisation style algorithms running in simulation and on external computers
global steering by magnetic, acoustic or optical fields
real-time imaging feedback

subsystems.name: Interface and clearance
subsystems.role: how clinicians see and steer the swarm, and how it leaves the body.
parts: MRI, ultrasound or X-ray tracking
external field generators
biodegradable or excretable materials

buildSteps.title: Pick the scale and architecture
buildSteps.detail: Choose between top-down micro-particles (roughly 1–100 micrometres, made by lithography) and bottom-up molecular structures (nanometres, made by chemical self-assembly). The two routes have almost nothing in common after this step.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the bodies
buildSteps.detail: Top-down: spin-coat a polymer, pattern it with photolithography or two-photon lithography, and release the particles. Bottom-up: synthesise DNA origami, peptides or polymer micelles that fold into a defined shape on their own.

buildSteps.title: Add a propulsion mechanism
buildSteps.detail: Coat one face of each particle with a catalyst or a magnetic metal so it moves under a fuel, a magnetic field or ultrasound — or give it a flexible tail that an oscillating field can beat.

buildSteps.title: Functionalise the surface
buildSteps.detail: Attach the cargo, targeting molecules and sensor chemistry by standard bioconjugation. This is also where biocompatibility and immune evasion are decided.

buildSteps.title: Give each agent local rules
buildSteps.detail: Encode simple if-then responses — follow a chemical gradient, change state when a threshold concentration is reached, release a marker after performing an action. No agent plans; the behaviour emerges.

buildSteps.title: Simulate the swarm
buildSteps.detail: Agent-based models test whether the local rules produce the intended collective behaviour, and how many agents are needed to overcome losses.

buildSteps.title: Test upward through model systems
buildSteps.detail: Microfluidic channels first, then cultured tissue, then small animals, verifying that the swarm reaches the target, acts and is cleared.

buildSteps.title: Build the clinical control rig
buildSteps.detail: A real treatment needs an imaging system and field generators working together, with a clinician able to steer, dose and stop the swarm in real time.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop
buildSteps.detail: Feedback from imaging adjusts the fields automatically until the task is complete — the hardest part, because tracking millions of micron-scale objects inside a moving body is currently beyond any imaging method.

prerequisites.tech: Micro- and nanofabrication at low cost
prerequisites.why: lithographic patterning already produces such particles, but not by the billion at a price a therapy could bear.
magnetically, acoustically and chemically driven micro-particles have been demonstrated in lab and small-animal studies, but control is crude and range is short.
agents must not trigger harmful immune reactions, and must break down or be excreted after the job.
without real-time position data for a whole swarm, no clinical procedure can be steered or stopped.
the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognised synthetic molecular machines that move on command, but these are molecules in solution, not free-swimming robots.
stigmergy and ant-colony-optimisation methods are mature in simulation and on centimetre-scale robots, but have not been run on millions of unreliable micro-agents.

pathway.milestone: individual micro-particles steered in lab dishes and small-animal studies; swarm algorithms tested in simulation and on centimetre-scale robot teams
pathway.unlocks: proof that a single agent can be made, moved and observed.

pathway.milestone: small swarms of hundreds to thousands performing one simple task in vivo, such as delivering a drug or breaking up a clot, with imaging feedback
pathway.unlocks: the first clinically meaningful swarm procedure.

pathway.milestone: biodegradable swarms that act, then dissolve, under closed-loop automated control
pathway.unlocks: regulatory and safety routes for human use, and repeatable manufacturing.

pathway.milestone: millions of agents coordinating by chemical signalling to reshape tissue, not just deliver cargo
pathway.unlocks: internal repair — heart valves, blocked vessels — without open surgery.

pathway.milestone: the same principles applied to micro-manufacturing, where swarms assemble objects atom by atom
pathway.unlocks: a bottom-up manufacturing route, if agent reliability and power delivery ever allow it.
